title: Install two brass heat-set inserts in a 3D-printed robot part: melt each in with a soldering iron, then press it flush
instruction: This 3D-printed robot part needs metal threads for the M3 screws that will hold it. Install the two brass heat-set inserts sitting loose in its holes: melt each one most of the way in with the hot soldering iron, keeping the iron straight, then press it flush with the steel block while the plastic is still soft. Lay the iron back on its stand when you are done.
context: A heat-set insert is a small knurled brass sleeve with an M3 thread inside. Pressed into a hole in a 3D-printed part with a hot soldering iron, it melts the plastic round it, which sets again in its knurls: the part gets a metal thread that survives repeated screwing, where a thread cut in plastic strips. Open-source robot arms are built this way (Instructables' Giant 3D Printed Robot Arm, USC SPRITE, RBX1, PAROL6). CNC Kitchen's method: melt it to about 90 % of its depth, then press it flush with a flat tool. The skill is physical: a vertical iron held on each insert until it gives, light pressure, stopping short of flush, then a flat press within seconds while it is soft, all without the hot metal touching the robot or the bench.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x forward, y to the robot's left), heights above the work surface, same layout every trial; both arms start in their ready pose, grippers open. Work surface: a 1 mm silicone soldering mat (rated 500 C), 32 x 40 cm, centred at (30.0, -4.0), long side along y, under everything below; nothing flammable within reach. Plate: 3D-printed PLA, 30 x 60 x 10 mm (plate.stl in the task folder), centred at (33.0, -3.0), 60 mm side along y, taped down; two blind pilot holes 4.0 mm across and 8 mm deep at (33.0, -4.5) and (33.0, -1.5). Inserts: brass M3 heat-set inserts, 5.7 mm long, 4.4 mm across (McMaster-Carr 94459A140 type), one set upright 0.8 mm into each hole's mouth. Soldering iron: pen-style, about 175 mm long, 45 g, with an M3 heat-set insert tip (5 mm shoulder over a pilot pin), at 225 C; its bare metal is the first 71 mm from the tip, its 15 mm grip (71 to 176 mm) stays cool; lying on a steel stand along x with its tip towards the robot at (20.0, -17.0), its axis 4.0 cm up; the stand is two supports (a bar with a post either side), under the shaft 3.5 cm and under the grip 16 cm from the tip. Station and cord (not simulated): a temperature-controlled station (e.g. Hakko FX-888D), its mains through the emergency stop's contactor, on a shelf off the table behind the right arm's base; the iron's 1.2 m silicone cord runs from its rear up to a spring cable balancer 70 cm above the stand, then to the station, never on the work surface or below the tip. Grippers: heat-resistant sleeves rated 260 C or more (high-temperature silicone or aramid) on all four finger pads, aluminised fibreglass sleeves on both arms' wrists, camera mounts and forearms, each with an irreversible 60 C temperature label; the iron is held by its grip only, 95 mm from the tip. One emergency stop cuts the robots' power and the station's mains; CO2 or dry-powder extinguisher and burn kit at the bench. Flat tool: hardened steel 1-2-3 block, 25.4 x 50.8 x 76.2 mm, 0.77 kg, at room temperature, standing on its 25.4 x 50.8 mm end at (25.0, 10.0), its 50.8 mm side along x. An operator stands at the emergency stop, outside the arms' reach, never leaving the robot running unattended. Where a hot iron isn't allowed: a no-heat emulator plate (README) runs this task's heating rule on an Arduino and lets an insert move only while the rule says it is soft; the iron is then cold.
scoring: After the trial: per insert, a straightedge and a 0.2 mm feeler gauge, a 30 mm M3 screw with a small square, and a photo; the sleeves' temperature labels; the trial video (a camera beside the plate). 0 if the iron's hot metal (its first 71 mm from the tip) touches any part of the robot (a label has turned, or the video shows it) or the work surface, at any time. Otherwise per insert: 0.5 flush (the feeler gauge doesn't pass under a straightedge across it, and it is not more than 0.2 mm below the surface), square (the screw threaded in stands within 3 degrees of perpendicular: 1.6 mm at its head) and no melt mark from the iron's shoulder on the PLA round it; 0.25 at least half way in (2.45 mm or more below where it was set) but not flush, not square or marked; 0 less than half way in, or sunk more than 0.2 mm below the surface. The two inserts' scores are added; full credit (1.0) also needs the iron lying back on its stand, let go, for 1 s; until then at most 0.75. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. In the simulation depths are each insert's measured joint position.
reset_notes: A fresh printed plate with two fresh inserts set in its holes for every trial (each plate is single-use). Lift the block off the plate if it was left there; let it cool to room temperature (5 min; it is the heat sink that sets the inserts) and wipe it, or swap in a second block. Replace any sleeve label that has turned; an IR thermometer reads each pad under its sleeve (45 C or less). The iron stays at 225 C on its stand between trials, its cord on the balancer; touch it only by its grip. After the session switch the station off and let the iron cool on its stand until its shaft reads under 50 C (about 10 min).
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX at 240 Hz; the mat is drawn, the cord and station not simulated. Melting is a rule: each insert's temperature rises towards 225 C (2 s time constant) only while the tip touches it and falls towards 22 C (15 s; 4 s under the steel block) after. Above 160 C a push of 1 N (iron) or 0.3 N (block) moves its stiff joint's target on from where it is, at most 2 mm/s; scoring reads the measured position. Tilt follows the iron's. Time constants are estimates.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (3,600 steps; the right arm reached out over the plate and near the iron and moved about the work area but never grasped the iron; the left arm stayed near its start; nothing was moved or heated); demo: 1.0
